content: Many women prefer to avoid pharmacological or invasive methods for managing pain during labor, which has led to the growing interest in complementary approaches such as aromatherapy. This review aimed to evaluate the current evidence regarding the effectiveness of aromatherapy in managing labor pain and its impact on maternal and perinatal outcomes. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared aromatherapy with placebo, no treatment, or other non-pharmacological pain management methods during labor. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases and trial registries up to October 31, 2010. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data, with additional information sought from study authors when necessary. Two trials involving a total of 535 women were included in the review. The findings showed no significant differences between the aromatherapy and control groups in terms of primary outcomes such as pain intensity, rates of assisted vaginal birth, or cesarean section. Specifically, for assisted vaginal birth, the risk ratio (RR) was 1.04 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48 to 2.28) in one trial with 513 women, and 0.83 (95% CI 0.06 to 11.70) in another trial with 22 women. For cesarean section, the RR was 0.98 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.94) in one trial with 513 women, and 2.54 (95% CI 0.11 to 56.25) in the smaller trial with 22 women. One trial reported a higher number of neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions in the control group compared to the aromatherapy group, with an RR of 0.08 (95% CI 0.00 to 1.42) for 513 women. However, this difference was not statistically significant. For secondary outcomes, no significant differences were observed between the groups in terms of the use of pharmacological pain relief, spontaneous vaginal delivery, or the length of labor and augmentation. For example, the RR for pharmacological pain relief was 0.35 (95% CI 0.04 to 3.32) in one trial with 513 women, and 2.50 (95% CI 0.31 to 20.45) in the smaller trial with 22 women. The RR for spontaneous vaginal delivery was 1.00 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.06) in one trial with 513 women, and 0.93 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.28) in the smaller trial. The RR for labor length and augmentation was 1.14 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.45) in one trial with 513 women. The included trials were assessed to have a low risk of bias. However, the overall evidence was limited due to the small number of studies and participants. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of aromatherapy for pain management during labor. Further high-quality research is needed before any clinical recommendations can be made regarding its effectiveness.
